tagline: Town streets, fields and memorials along the route of revolution
intro: The Battle Road Scenic Byway moves between developed town streets, thick foliage and open fields in Arlington, Lexington, Lincoln and Concord. The Federal Highway Administration lists it as a National Scenic Byway, recognizing a corridor of Revolutionary history, literature and environmental thought. Its driving route is distinct from the five-mile Battle Road Trail, which winds through fields and forests in Minute Man National Historical Park. The corridor plan describes preservation of its historic, scenic, cultural and recreational resources as the purpose of state designation.

On April 19, 1775, British troops marched to Concord to seize military supplies; militia attacked their retreat along Battle Road. The corridor continued as a major travel route, with sections incorporated into a state highway. Postwar suburban and military development threatened the colonial landscape, prompting a recommendation for a national park, established in 1959. The four towns supported state byway designation in 2006 as another step in its preservation.

Travel northwest from Arlington along Massachusetts Avenue to Lexington Battle Green, then continue toward North Great Road in Lincoln. The Paul Revere capture memorial precedes Concord, where the route reaches Monument Square and turns toward Monument and Liberty streets. The 2011 corridor plan ends the drive at the Buttrick Mansion and Muster Field, near North Bridge.

moments.title: Lexington Battle Green
moments.text: Lexington residents bought this ground for militia training in 1711, raising the money by subscription. On April 19, 1775, local militiamen came out of Buckman Tavern and formed two rows on the common to face British troops. The triangular green is now a public park. Near its western corner, a granite obelisk erected in 1799 commemorates the Revolution. In 1835, seven militiamen killed in the battle were reburied within its iron fence. At the eastern corner, Henry Hudson Kitson’s statue represents Captain John Parker, leader of the Lexington militia. It was erected in 1900.

moments.title: Paul Revere Capture Site
moments.text: A monument on the Battle Road Trail marks where Paul Revere was captured during his midnight ride. The warning continued without him: Samuel Prescott escaped a British patrol by jumping his horse over a wall and riding into the woods. At Hartwell Tavern, Prescott alerted Ephraim Hartwell, who sent Violet, a woman he enslaved, to warn his son’s household. Mary Hartwell carried the message to Captain William Smith of the Lincoln minutemen. Prescott reached Concord. The Lincoln minutemen received the warning in time to reach Old North Bridge before the British, extending the relay from households to the militia.

moments.title: North Bridge and Muster Field
moments.text: The wooden footbridge over the Concord River dates to 1956, an approximate replica of the bridge used in the 1775 fighting. During that battle, militia saw smoke rising from Concord and believed British troops were burning the town. They advanced toward the bridge; after a British volley, Major John Buttrick ordered them to fire. The Americans returned fire and the British retreated to Concord. A new crossing downstream made North Bridge obsolete in 1793, and the town abandoned the old road. No bridge stood here for the next eighty-two years. The present bridge was extensively restored in 2005.
